The main 'Empezar' button leads to a drill that first asks the user to find a book or article to read aloud. That contradicts the promise of a quick first practice and would stall someone with nothing to hand.

C.name: track chooser in the panel plus Mínimo

notes.summary: [C] wins because it asks me in plain words whether I want to sing or speak, which are my two real goals, and then gives one obvious 3-minute button that needs no preparation, with little else competing for my tap. It would be better if the unexplained jargon 'Trinos' were replaced or explained in simple words, like 'vibrar los labios', and if the top bar were less cluttered (Pro, Cuenta, English, Tour). [A] falls last because its first practice needs reading material that nobody warned me about, and it repeats the same action under three labels.

[C] wins because it lets the visitor pick what suits them (Cantar / Hablar, with plain examples), then offers one clear, prep-free 3-minute start. Secondary options are reduced to quiet links. Its biggest gains would come from a headline that says what the practice is, a 'no book or sheet music needed' line like [B]'s, and plainer wording than 'Trinos'. [B] is a close second but assumes singing and crowds the first screen. [A]'s main button leads to a drill that needs a book, and its labels are misleading.

[C] wins because a first-time, less confident user sees only one question with two large, plainly described choices and then one large button with its duration. By the behaviour notes, that button starts a 3-minute routine that needs nothing prepared, and nothing else on the first screen competes with it. [B] is close on reassurance but adds clutter and hides the speaking path behind a small, jargon-labelled link. [A] sends users to a drill that needs a book and gives three differently named buttons for the same action. [C] would improve most by adding a visible checkmark or 'Elegido' label to the selected option, and by replacing 'Trinos' with plain language such as 'vibrar los labios'.

loop-copy.title: Today's basics for someone who practised the last three days

notes.summary: [C] wins because I can see what today is and tap the big green 'Empezar básicos' right under the title, with nothing to read in between. That suits someone impatient on a phone. It would be even better if the 'Continuar práctica' and 'Iniciar sesión guiada' buttons were less prominent or moved further down, and if the Mínimo/Esencial/Clase chips clearly said whether you can tap them, so the green button is the only obvious action.

[C] wins because its hierarchy does exactly the job: a short label, a plain headline saying what today's practice is and how long it takes, then the start button immediately below it, highest on the phone screen. [B] is close and more specific about the 1:30 + 1:30 sequence, but its extra nested box and repeated duration add clutter. [C] would improve most by adding the sequence as a light subline (e.g. 'Trinos 1:30 → solfeo 1:30') without a nested box, and by keeping the laptop button as large as it is on the phone.

[B] wins because its large title states the two steps and their lengths, and one short, reassuring line leads to a big, high start button. An older or unsure learner knows what will happen and can start without help. [C] is close and even simpler, but it hides the two-part structure and shows competing play-style buttons on the phone. [B] would improve most by moving '3 minutos' out of the small capitals and into the large title or the button label (for example '▶ Empezar · 3 min'). Writing the durations as '1 min 30' rather than '1:30' would avoid a clock-time misreading.

[B] does the job best on the phone I actually use: the one compact row stays at the top, so I can always move between Practicar, Plan and Historial, leaves the most room for the exercise, and puts Pro, Cuenta, English and Tour behind one clear 'Más' tap. It would be even better with a '▾' arrow or a different look on 'Más' so it doesn't look like another tab, and with a thinner pinned bar when the phone is sideways.

[B] wins because it has the smallest pinned header on a portrait phone, the three main destinations are always reachable, and the secondary items are behind 'Más'. That best balances navigation against space for practice. [C]'s scroll-away header gives space back only by hiding the nav, and [A]'s always-visible third row eats the screen. [B] would improve most with a chevron on 'Más' so the menu is discoverable. In landscape, where all three show the same full row, it should also shrink or auto-hide the pinned header.

[B] does the job best: its compact, single pinned row keeps the three sections one tap away at all times while giving the most screen to practice, with large, well-spaced targets and little to take in. [C] is more predictable ('Más ▾', visible app name), but its header scrolls away, which strands older users further down the page. [A] hides nothing but spends too much permanent space on two rows of pills that all look alike. [B] would improve most by adding an arrow to 'Más' and a visible app name or label beside the music-note icon.

done-card.title: Home after today's basics are done

B.name: one-line done strip, no level chips

notes.summary: [A] wins because its done box is roomy and says in one plain sentence that I can do more or just come back tomorrow, with a big, obvious 'Otra vuelta' button and level choices that show minutes. That feels calm, not pushy. [B] is simpler, but its done box is cramped on the phone and 'Continuar práctica' makes me doubt I'm done. [A] would improve most by fixing the '1 min' vs '3 min' mismatch, removing the duplicate 'Hoy: Mínimo' chip, and keeping the extra buttons (Continuar práctica, Iniciar sesión guiada, Ruta) out of the finished-today view.

[A] wins: on the phone its done card is clean and legible, and it says in words that stopping is fine ('Si no, hasta mañana'). It also offers real, optional ways to do more (repeat today's routine or pick a longer level), all styled as secondary buttons. [B] is calmer, but on the phone its done card wraps badly, and the only extra it offers is repeating the same routine. [A] would improve most by dropping the 'Hoy: Mínimo' chip, which repeats the done card, and by merging its stacked desktop action rows so less of the first screen goes to optional actions.

[A] wins because its done card is big and clean on the phone, and its plain-language line 'Si quieres más, elige otro nivel. Si no, hasta mañana.' gives an older or less confident user explicit permission to stop and a clear path to more, backed by a large full-width tap target. Its main weakness is clutter: it would improve most by dropping the redundant highlighted 'Hoy: Mínimo' chip and moving the streak/week-goal proof higher so 'counted' shows on the first phone screen, as it does in [B].

record-strip.title: The practice record on a phone

notes.summary: [B] wins because it fits my day count, the week dots and the weekly progress bar into one compact strip that I can see on the first screen of a normal phone, without pushing everything else down. [A] spends space on a big heading and the vague 'Próximo hito: 7', so the weekly progress falls off the screen. [B] would get better with simpler wording for the weekly line, for example 'Esta semana: 2 días (meta 3 a 5)', and a plainer phrase than 'día de descanso guardado'.

[B] wins because it puts the day count, the week's dots, the streak and this week's goal progress into one compact card. It fits on the first screen of a standard phone and keeps the rest of the page close. [A] spreads the same content vertically, so the weekly progress falls below the fold. [B] would improve most with a less cramped 'días cantados' label and some visible way to change the weekly goal on phones, such as a small edit link.

[B] wins because it shows both the total days sung and this week's progress (with a text equivalent, not colour alone) on the first screen of a normal phone, without pushing the rest of the page down. [A] is easier on the eyes but hides the weekly progress below the fold. [B] would improve most by making the 'días cantados' label and the day letters/circles a little larger and less cramped, and by clarifying why the total (3) differs from this week's check marks (2).

step-end.title: The moment a guided step's time runs out

blocking: beginner

When the time ends there's no message and no next-step button on screen. The 'En vivo' badge stays green and the mic stays on, so it looks like the exercise is still running. The action to continue is below the fold, and I couldn't find it without scrolling and guessing.
designer

There is no sign that the step has ended apart from '00:00', and 'En vivo' still shows as live with the mic on. The next-step action is off the first screen, so the learner may keep singing or not know how to move on.
access

At 0:00 nothing on the first screen says the exercise has ended. The green 'En vivo' badge stays next to '00:00' and the mic stays on, which suggests it is still running. The button to go to the next step is off-screen below the fold, and nothing hints that it is there.

notes.summary: [B] wins by a wide margin: when the time is up it says so clearly ('¡Listo!', 'Paso 1 de 2 ✓') and puts one large button with the next exercise's name in the middle of the screen, so I'd know what to tap right away on my phone. [A] looks almost the same at 0:00 as during the exercise, the mic stays live and the way forward is out of sight. [B] would be better with a plainer label than 'Puntuar', for example 'Calificar cómo me fue'.

[B] wins clearly. At 0:00 it replaces the practice area with a plain 'done' message and one large button that names the next exercise. The learner knows the step is over and can move on with one tap, while '30 s más' and 'Puntuar' are still offered as secondary options. It would improve most by using the same term in the banner and the overlay ('paso' vs 'ejercicio'). It could also show a small countdown or hint that the mic has stopped, so the end of the step is fully clear.

[B] wins clearly. It says in words that the step is done ('¡Listo!', 'PASO 1 DE 2 ✓'), dims everything else, and gives one large, high-contrast, centred button that names the next exercise. An older user can move on without help. [A] shows only '00:00' beside a still-green 'En vivo' badge, leaves the mic on, and hides the next-step button below the fold. It also has overlapping controls on the phone. [B] would improve most with a larger, higher-contrast 'Paso 1 de 2 completado' line and a clearer label than 'Puntuar' (for example 'Puntuar este ejercicio').

notes.summary: [B] wins because it hides the site header in landscape. That leaves the timer, the exercise card and the Detener controls all visible at once in both the guided session and the single exercise. [A] covers the timer in one case and a button and some text in the other. The biggest improvement for [B] would be a small pause/end control for the guided session, plus moving the timer pill so it doesn't overlap the card title.

[B] does the job the brief sets. It removes the site header in landscape, so the timer, the full practice card and the singing controls all fit on the first screen without layers covering each other. [A] buries the live timer under a sticky header in the guided session, and its selector bar covers the practice feedback. [B] would improve most by moving the timer badge off the card heading and by putting a small Pausar/Terminar for the session, plus the MIC control, into the empty band above the controls row.

[B] does what the brief asks. In both landscape screenshots the practice card, timer and singing controls fit on one screen, and the only overlap is the timer over the card heading, which is minor. [A] keeps the site header and breadcrumbs, and they hide the timer in the guided session and cover part of the exercise content. [B] would improve most by moving the timer so it no longer covers the card heading and by giving the guided session a small visible Pausar/Terminar control, so an older user is not left with only '← Atrás' to get out.

blocking: beginner

The instructions say 'Quédate en el carril verde', but no lane is green. The target note (A2) looks the same as the other plain dashed rows, and several other lanes are highlighted gold, so the wrong lines look like targets.

The instructions say 'Quédate en el carril verde', but no green lane is drawn. The target lane (A2) looks the same as every other dashed lane, and the only green on screen is the G key on the keyboard, which is not the target. This steers the user toward the wrong note.

[B] wins because the only thing I need to do, start, is a big, full-width green 'Empezar' button with nothing competing next to it, so I tap it in the first seconds. [B] does the job best. Its full-width, tall Empezar button is the one obvious primary action on the first screen at both phone sizes, and it is easy to tap with one thumb. [A]'s small left-aligned Empezar is smaller than a secondary button and crowded by a slider and unlabelled controls. [B] would improve most by filling or collapsing the blank gap left on the small phone, labelling or removing the empty bar above Empezar, and fixing the clipped heading and instruction text.

[B] does the job better. Its Empezar button is large, full-width, high-contrast and nearly alone, so an older or unsure user sees at once how to start and can do it in one tap. [A] crowds a small Empezar button among a mic slider and unlabeled octave, checkbox and piano controls. [B] would improve most by fixing the missing or blank instructions area on small phones, removing or labeling the empty bar above the button, and giving the clipped step list a visible scroll cue.

[B] wins because it is the only one where a beginner like me can understand what an exercise is before tapping it. [B] wins because it is the only one that explains what each exercise is. The biggest improvement would be tighter descriptions that say something new in one line and never repeat the title or cut off mid-word, which would also shorten rows. [B] wins because it is the only design that answers 'what is this exercise?'. Its short plain-language description under each jargon-heavy title lets an older or unsure learner choose with confidence, while keeping large full-row tap targets and a predictable layout. blocking: beginner

[B] wins because it is the only one that answers 'which of these are in my daily basics?' (the 'Hoy en tus básicos' badges), and its group names say what each set is for. [B] would improve most by replacing the stale Básico/Avanzado intro line with copy that matches its groups, and by pulling today's basics into a short strip or filter at the top instead of scattering badges deep in the list.

[B] wins because it is the only design that tells the singer which exercises are in their daily basics, with a text badge that does not depend on colour. The biggest improvements to [B] would be to rewrite the helper sentence so it matches the 'Clase del mes' / 'Calentamientos y técnica' groups, and to put the daily basics near the top (a 'Mis básicos de hoy' filter chip or a pinned strip) instead of leaving the badges deep in the list. blocking: beginner
After you pick a focus and press 'Iniciar / continuar semana', the page offers no way to reach an exercise. A beginner doesn't know where to practise next, so the page stops short of its job.

The page has no route from the chosen focus to any exercise, so after pressing start the learner is stranded on the Plan page with nothing to practise.

B.name: one focus, its exercises, days counted

notes.summary: [B] wins because I understand it in seconds: a few focus choices, one clear 'Empezar esta semana' button, nothing else in the way, and the exercises open directly so I actually get to practise. [A] buries the start button under 17 chips full of jargon plus review forms I can't use yet, and it never takes me to an exercise. [B] would improve most by showing a mix of singing and speaking options before 'Ver otros 12', using plainer names (for example 'Voz más clara' instead of 'Resonancia y velo del paladar'), and keeping the start button on the first phone screen.

[B] wins because it gives this job one clear path: show a few focus areas with the rest one tap away, then one obvious start button. Everything fits on the first desktop screen and is one short scroll away on a phone. According to the notes, its exercises open directly and days practised are counted automatically. [A] buries its vaguely labelled start button under 17 chips and an early, disabled review form, and it offers no way to reach an exercise. [B] would improve most by making the week markers bigger, proper tap targets without the orphaned '12', and by picking its first five chips to suit the learner's goal (singing or speaking).

[B] wins for older adults. It asks for one decision from a short list and puts the start button right below it. It fits on one desktop screen, and per the behaviour notes it links straight to exercises, so the learner actually gets to practising. [A] buries the start button under 17 options and a stack of empty sections, and never links to exercises. [B] would improve most by making 'Ver otros 12' a clear button, giving week numbers visible tap-sized targets, and repeating 'Semana 1' in the card for orientation.

[B] wins because it does all three parts of the job: a clear practice total with a calendar, a recency-ordered list with human relative dates, and rows that open the exercise so the learner can resume. What would most improve [B] is shrinking the calendar on the phone, or moving the top 'Lo último que practicaste' row (or an explicit 'Continuar' button) above it, and labelling the month and the period that '3 días' covers.

[B] wins because it covers the whole job. It shows a clear total ('3 días cantados'), lists the latest practice with friendly relative dates, and lets you resume with one tap on a big row. [A] leads with an empty recordings block, has no summary and no visible way to resume. [B] would improve most by marking practised days with more than colour (e.g. a tick), labelling the '3× · 7/10' meta (e.g. '3 veces · nota 7/10'), and making the resume action explicit with a word like 'Seguir' next to the arrow.

B.name: one plan, interval toggle, plain benefits

notes.summary: [B] wins because in a few seconds I understand what Pro adds (in plain Spanish), what it costs and that payments are not open yet, so I should keep practising for free. It would improve most by showing the monthly price without a tap and giving me something I can do now, like a free trial or a clear 'Seguir practicando gratis' button. [A] buries Pro under the free card, uses jargon and has two competing dead-end buttons. The 'payments not live yet, keep practising free' message sits right beside the only button, so nobody is left wondering what happened or what to do next. It would improve most by making the Mensual/Anual and payment selections clearly visible (checkmark, strong outline, or 'Seleccionado' text) and by showing the monthly price next to the switch.
